query: Consider the following context: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for next-generation nuclear applications, particularly fusion reactors, due to their excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In that context, which material can be used for low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components (PFCs) in fusion reactors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy whose composition is tailored to minimize high‐activation elements while retaining refractory elements can serve as an effective low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional tungsten-based plasma-facing materials, which although possessing high melting temperatures, suffer from brittleness and issues associated with neutron-induced activation.
generation.intervention: Use integrated computational alloy design combined with high-throughput experimental synthesis to adjust the alloy composition of a refractory HEA by selectively reducing high-activation species and incorporating low-activation refractory elements.
generation.conditions: Exposed to high-temperature plasma conditions (≥1000 K) and simulated fusion-relevant neutron irradiation fluxes.
generation.structural_mediator: Optimized phase stability and grain structure resulting from the modified alloy composition, which promotes the formation of a uniform microstructure and inhibits deleterious defect evolution under irradiation.
generation.mechanism: The modified composition minimizes the generation of long-lived radioactive isotopes upon neutron irradiation while enhancing high-temperature mechanical performance. Reduction of high-activation species coupled with reinforcement of defect stability reduces embrittlement and irradiation-induced damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: The engineered refractory HEA will show both improved mechanical integrity at high temperatures and significantly lower activation levels compared to traditional tungsten-based materials, making it a promising candidate for PFC applications.
generation.baseline: Standard tungsten-based plasma-facing materials known for their high melting temperature but limited by brittle failure and higher activation after neutron exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is bounded by the ability to successfully control the alloy composition and phase stability in a multicomponent HEA system under prolonged operational conditions in a fusion reactor environment. Uncertainties remain regarding the full scale-up of synthesis and long-term oxidation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While improvements in activation and mechanical performance are anticipated, the quantitative reduction in activation and long-term irradiation and oxidation stability under reactor conditions remain to be rigorously validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize samples of the proposed refractory HEA with the tailored low-activation composition and expose them to high-temperature plasma conditions (≥1000 K) and simulated high-flux neutron irradiation in a controlled test reactor. Compare the typical metrics with standard tungsten-based PFC materials.
measurements: High-temperature tensile and creep strength tests pre- and post-irradiation
Microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) to assess defect formation and grain stability
Activation level measurements via gamma spectroscopy or other radiometric methods
Oxidation rate and surface morphology analysis after thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not exhibit both statistically significant improvements in high-temperature mechanical properties and reduced neutron activation levels compared to tungsten-based materials, or if it shows rapid oxidation or deleterious phase instabilities under test conditions, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Key components in magnetic fusion reactors, such as the divertor or the plasma-facing materials (PFMs), are required to have stringent properties including low activation, high melting point, good thermomechanical properties, low sputter erosion, and low tritium retention/codeposition. They must operate at high temperature (≥1000 K) for long durations (>10 7 s), without failure or extensive erosion while exposed to large plasma heat and an intense mixture of ionized and energetic neutral species of hydrogen isotopes (D and T), He ash (fluxes, >10 24 m −2 s −1 ), and neutrons ( [1] ). Tungsten (W) is the leading PFM candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rates, and small tritium retention. These advantages are unfortunately coupled with very low fracture toughness characterized by brittle transgranular and intergranular failure regimes, which severely restrict the useful operating temperature window and also create a range of fabrication difficulties. Furthermore, blistering at moderate temperature (<800 K) by D and He ( [2] , [3] ) and the formation of pits, holes, and bubbles by He at higher temperature (>1600 K) ( [4] ) have all been observed. The attractiveness of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as structural materials stems from their outstanding mechanical properties, thermal stability, wear resistance and corrosion performance in hostile environments [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ]. Recently, refractory high-entropy alloys have received significant attention in relation to high-temperature application in aerospace, defense, and nuclear power generation industries [ [6] ]. In fact, they were designated to replace traditional Ni-based super-alloys in applications such as gas turbines, heat exchangers, aerospace propulsion components, rocket engine nozzle [ [7] ]. HEAs are multicomponent systems that are composed from a small number of principal elements. They are usually composed from at least five elements with individual atomic concentrations that range between 5% and 35%. HEAs can produce solid phase solutions, mainly due to their configurational entropy and ability to be adequately synthesized [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
